reference.source: Smith's Recognizable Patterns of Human Malformation
clinicalPearls: An autosomal recessive primordial growth disorder causing pre- and postnatal proportionate short stature with normal intelligence
Caused by biallelic mutations in one of three genes: CUL7, OBSL1 or CCDC8 (the initials of which give the syndrome its name)
Birth length and weight are low and severe short stature persists, but head circumference is relatively preserved, giving a relatively large head appearance
Facial features include a triangular face, a prominent forehead, a fleshy-tipped nose, full lips and a pointed chin (historically described as a 'gloomy' facial appearance)
Skeletal features include slender long bones with thin cortices, tall (flat, wedge-shaped) vertebral bodies and slender ribs on radiographs
Growth-hormone testing is usually normal and children generally respond poorly to growth-hormone therapy, distinguishing it from classic growth-hormone deficiency
It is an important differential of Silver-Russell syndrome, but 3M syndrome lacks the marked body asymmetry and has a distinct radiographic and molecular basis
Diagnosis is confirmed by molecular testing of CUL7, OBSL1 and CCDC8
reference.pathophysiology: 3M syndrome is caused by loss of function of components of a protein complex (CUL7, OBSL1 and CCDC8) that regulates cell growth, cytoskeletal organisation and protein turnover, and interacts with pathways controlling growth and the response to growth factors. CUL7 is part of an E3 ubiquitin-ligase complex, while OBSL1 and CCDC8 form a scaffold that maintains the stability and localisation of the complex. Disruption impairs normal cellular growth signalling from before birth, producing severe primordial short stature with characteristic skeletal changes, while sparing cognitive development.
additionalDifferentials: Microcephalic primordial dwarfism syndromes (e.g. MOPD, though head size differs)
additionalInvestigations: Molecular testing of CUL7, OBSL1 and CCDC8 to confirm the diagnosis
Serial growth measurements with attention to relatively preserved head circumference
Skeletal radiographs to document slender long bones, tall vertebrae and slender ribs
Growth-hormone and IGF-1 axis assessment to exclude classic growth-hormone deficiency
Assessment for hypogonadism where indicated in affected males
Genetic counselling given autosomal recessive inheritance
redFlags: Failure to thrive or feeding difficulty in infancy requiring nutritional support
Misdiagnosis leading to prolonged, ineffective growth-hormone treatment
Airway or anaesthetic concerns related to facial and skeletal features
reference.prognosis: Cognition and life expectancy are normal; the main issue is marked short stature, which responds poorly to growth hormone, so management focuses on accurate diagnosis, realistic counselling and monitoring for skeletal and endocrine issues.
pitfalls: Labelling the child as growth-hormone deficient and expecting a good response to therapy
Confusing 3M syndrome with Silver-Russell syndrome without noting the absence of asymmetry
Overlooking the characteristic radiographic features that support the diagnosis
Failing to recognise autosomal recessive inheritance and its recurrence risk
references: Smith's Recognizable Patterns of Human Malformation
